bio_full: Rogers was born in Florence to an Anglo-Italian family that moved to England in 1939. He studied at the Architectural Association and at Yale, where he met Norman Foster, with whom he formed Team 4 in 1963. With Renzo Piano he won the competition for the Centre Pompidou in 1971. His later firm, now Rogers Stirk Harbour and Partners, designed the Lloyd's building (1986), the Millennium Dome, Terminal 4 of Madrid Barajas Airport and the Leadenhall Building. He sat in the House of Lords and championed compact, sustainable cities.

Rogers turned buildings inside out, placing structure, lifts, stairs and service ducts on the exterior to free flexible open floors and to give the city a lively, legible machine. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2007.

name: Renzo Piano
bio: Italian architect, co-designer of the Centre Pompidou, whose later museums and towers, among them the Shard in London, combine lightness, craft and engineering.
bio_full: Piano grew up in a family of builders in Genoa and studied at the Milan Polytechnic. After the Centre Pompidou with Richard Rogers, he founded the Renzo Piano Building Workshop, with offices in Genoa and Paris. Its works include the Menil Collection in Houston, Kansai International Airport, the Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre in New Caledonia, the Potsdamer Platz redevelopment in Berlin, the California Academy of Sciences, the Shard in London and the Whitney Museum in New York.

Piano's architecture is detailed with craftsmanlike care, uses light roofs and filtered daylight, and seeks to integrate engineering and context rather than impose a single style. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1998 and was named a senator for life in Italy in 2013.

name: Norman Foster
bio: British architect whose firm designed the HSBC headquarters in Hong Kong, the glass dome of the Reichstag and 30 St Mary Axe, leading high-tech and sustainable design.
bio_full: Foster grew up in a working-class family near Manchester, studied at the University of Manchester and at Yale, and founded Team 4 with Richard Rogers before setting up Foster Associates in 1967. Early works such as the Willis Faber and Dumas building in Ipswich and the Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts were followed by the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank headquarters (1986), Stansted Airport, the Reichstag dome in Berlin (1999), the Great Court of the British Museum, the Millau Viaduct with the engineer Michel Virlogeux, and 30 St Mary Axe in London (2004). Foster and Partners became one of the largest architecture firms in the world.

Foster's buildings emphasise lightweight structure, prefabrication, daylight and natural ventilation, and his practice has made energy performance a central design concern. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1999 and a life peerage.

name: Frank Gehry
bio: Canadian-American architect of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall, whose sculptural, computer-designed forms changed the image of architecture.
bio_full: Frank Owen Goldberg moved from Toronto to Los Angeles in 1947, studied architecture at the University of Southern California and city planning at Harvard, and opened his own office in 1962. His renovation of his own house in Santa Monica (1978), wrapped in chain-link fencing and corrugated metal, made his name. He then designed the Vitra Design Museum in Germany, the Dancing House in Prague, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997), the Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003), the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris and many other buildings worldwide.

Gehry worked from crumpled paper and hand-made models, and his office adapted software from the aerospace industry to design and fabricate complex curved surfaces, a revolution in how buildings are made. The success of Bilbao in reviving its city gave rise to the term 'Bilbao effect' for iconic cultural buildings. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1989.

name: Zaha Hadid
bio: Iraqi-British architect, the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, whose dynamic, flowing buildings range from the Vitra Fire Station to the Heydar Aliyev Center.
bio_full: Hadid studied mathematics at the American University of Beirut and architecture at the Architectural Association in London, where she worked with Rem Koolhaas. For years her explosive, painted competition designs, such as The Peak in Hong Kong (1983), were celebrated but unbuilt. Her first major building was the Vitra Fire Station (1993), followed by the Rosenthal Center in Cincinnati, the Phaeno Science Centre, MAXXI in Rome, the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics, the Guangzhou Opera House and the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku. She won the Pritzker Prize in 2004 and died suddenly at sixty-five.

Influenced by the Russian avant-garde, especially Malevich, Hadid began with fragmented, angular forms and moved, with her partner Patrik Schumacher and digital tools, toward continuous, fluid surfaces. Her success as a woman in a male-dominated profession made her a role model, while some commissions for authoritarian states drew criticism.

name: Daniel Libeskind
bio: Polish-American architect whose Jewish Museum Berlin turned architecture into a medium of memory.
bio_full: Libeskind, the son of Holocaust survivors, studied music in Israel and New York before turning to architecture at the Cooper Union. He was known for theoretical drawings and teaching until he won the competition for the Jewish Museum Berlin in 1989, which opened in 2001. His later works include the Imperial War Museum North in Manchester, the extension of the Denver Art Museum and the Royal Ontario Museum, and in 2003 he won the competition for the master plan of the World Trade Center site in New York.

Libeskind's buildings are made of sharp, intersecting volumes and slashed openings, intended to express rupture and absence. He was one of the architects shown at the 1988 Deconstructivist Architecture exhibition at MoMA.

name: Rem Koolhaas
bio: Dutch architect and writer, founder of OMA and author of Delirious New York, whose buildings include the Seattle Central Library and the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing.
bio_full: Koolhaas worked as a journalist and screenwriter before studying at the Architectural Association in London and at Cornell. In 1975 he founded the Office for Metropolitan Architecture with Elia and Zoe Zenghelis and Madelon Vriesendorp, and published Delirious New York (1978), a 'retroactive manifesto' for Manhattan. OMA's works include the Kunsthal in Rotterdam, the Euralille master plan, the Maison à Bordeaux, the Casa da Música in Porto, the Seattle Central Library (2004) and the CCTV Headquarters (2012). He taught at Harvard, wrote S,M,L,XL with Bruce Mau, and in 2014 directed the Venice Architecture Biennale.

Koolhaas treats architecture as a response to the forces of the modern metropolis, programme and global capitalism rather than as an exercise in style. His research studios at Harvard examined shopping, the Pearl River Delta and Lagos, and many leading architects trained at OMA. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2000.

name: Santiago Calatrava
bio: Spanish architect and engineer of bridges, stations and the City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia, whose white structures recall skeletons and wings.
bio_full: Calatrava studied architecture in Valencia and civil engineering at the ETH in Zurich, where he wrote a doctoral thesis on folding structures and opened his practice in 1981. He designed the Stadelhofen station in Zurich, the Alamillo Bridge in Seville, the Lyon-Saint Exupéry airport station, the Milwaukee Art Museum extension, the City of Arts and Sciences in his native Valencia, the Turning Torso in Malmö and the World Trade Center Transportation Hub in New York.

Calatrava's work merges sculpture, architecture and engineering in white steel and concrete, with forms derived from his studies of the human body and animals. His buildings are admired for their drama and criticised for cost overruns and practical problems.

name: Herzog & de Meuron
bio: Basel practice of Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron, known for Tate Modern, the Beijing National Stadium and the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg.
bio_full: Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron, both born in Basel in 1950, studied together at the ETH in Zurich under Aldo Rossi among others and founded their practice in Basel in 1978. Early works such as the Signal Box in Basel and the Ricola storage building attracted attention for their surfaces. The conversion of Bankside Power Station into Tate Modern (2000) brought international fame, followed by the de Young Museum in San Francisco, the Allianz Arena in Munich, the Beijing National Stadium with Ai Weiwei (2008), the Elbphilharmonie (2017) and M+ in Hong Kong.

Herzog & de Meuron have no signature style; each project begins with experiments in material, from printed glass and copper bands to concrete and stone, and they often collaborate with artists. They received the Pritzker Prize in 2001.
